touches.text: The bus makes this messaging inspectable, the messages show on the bus' web panel as a "Murderbot Diaries" "Public Feed" the operator can review for purposes such as diagnostics.
Own foundational components (bus, ground loop, rack, shims, scheduler, launcher). The scheduler is the base shim's (5.8); harbor_master is CodeMother's (10.8).
A device owns its state: only the device writes under its own ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/ tree.
A device holds machines and uses tools (from cairn/tools/). A tool's data for that device lives under the device: ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/tools/<tool>/
Transient: the transient tree (what the logging tree becomes).

Cairn owns all of ~/.cairn/ and delegates each ~/.cairn/devices/ subtree to its device. Everything outside devices/ (~/.cairn/logging/ and the rest) is Cairn's, so every log is Cairn's and Cairn cleans them up in sleep. Transient things are files there. Trouble tickets are logging items.
Cairn's own sleep has a lot to do, including clearing the logging tree of things older than 30 days.

conflicts.text: An instance is declared by its folder existing in class-space: cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/ (one address in two roots). Declared = the folders; running = which of those are in the rack. (Q#18, Akien 2026-11-04)
conflicts.why: The outline establishes in 5.6.2.4 that instances are declared with structure cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/ ('one address in two roots'), with instance folder first in both class-space and instance-space. The pattern is confirmed by 2.2.7 (tool data: ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/tools/<tool>/). The ticket reverses the order, putting the machine folder before instance, which contradicts this principle.
